paragraphs: On the way to Ivan’s he had to pass the house where Katerina Ivanovna was living. There were lights in the windows. He stopped suddenly and decided to go in. He had not seen Katerina Ivanovna for more than a week. But now it occurred to him that Ivan might be with her, especially on the eve of that terrible day. He rang, and as he climbed the staircase, which was dimly lit by a Chinese lantern, he saw a man coming down. When they met, he recognized his brother. So Ivan was just leaving Katerina Ivanovna.
“Oh, it’s only you,” said Ivan drily. “Well, goodbye! You’re going up to her?”
“Yes.”
“I wouldn’t advise it. She’s upset, and you’ll upset her more.”
A door above was flung open at once, and a voice suddenly cried out:
“No, no! Alexey Fyodorovitch, have you come from him?”
“Yes, I’ve been with him.”
“Did he send any message for me? Come up, Alyosha. And you, Ivan Fyodorovitch, you must come back, you must. Do you hear?”
Katya’s voice had such a commanding note that Ivan, after a moment’s hesitation, decided to go back up with Alyosha.
“She was listening,” he muttered angrily to himself, but Alyosha heard it.
“Excuse me for keeping my greatcoat on,” said Ivan, as he went into the drawing-room. “I won’t sit down. I won’t stay more than a minute.”

“Sit down, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” said Katerina Ivanovna, though she stayed on her feet herself. She had changed very little in that time, but there was an ominous gleam in her dark eyes. Alyosha remembered afterwards that she had struck him as especially beautiful at that moment.
“What did he ask you to tell me?”

“Only one thing,” said Alyosha, looking her straight in the face. “He asks you to spare yourself, and not to say anything at the trial about what” (he got a little confused) “... went on between you ... when you first got to know each other ... in that town.”

“Ah! That I bowed down to the ground to him for that money!” She broke into a bitter laugh. “Why, is he afraid for me, or for himself? He asks me to spare—who? Him or myself? Tell me, Alexey Fyodorovitch!”
Alyosha watched her closely, trying to understand her.
“Both you and him,” he answered quietly.
“I’m glad to hear it,” she snapped out spitefully, and suddenly she blushed.
“You don’t know me yet, Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she said, in a threatening tone. “And I don’t know myself yet. Maybe after I’m questioned tomorrow, you’ll want to trample me underfoot.”
“You will give your evidence honorably,” said Alyosha. “That’s all that’s needed.”

“Women are often dishonorable,” she snarled. “Only an hour ago I was thinking how afraid I was to touch that monster ... as if he were a reptile ... but no, he’s still a human being to me! But did he do it? Is he the murderer?” she cried suddenly, hysterically, turning quickly to Ivan. Alyosha saw at once that she had asked Ivan the same question before, perhaps only a moment before he came in, and not for the first time but for the hundredth, and that they had ended by quarreling.

“I’ve been to see Smerdyakov.... It was you, you who persuaded me that he murdered his father. You’re the only one I believed!” she went on, still speaking to Ivan. He gave her a kind of forced smile. Alyosha started at her tone. He had never suspected such familiar intimacy between them.
“Well, that’s enough of this, anyway,” Ivan cut the conversation short. “I’m going. I’ll come tomorrow.” And turning at once, he walked out of the room and went straight down the stairs.
With an imperious gesture, Katerina Ivanovna seized Alyosha by both hands.

“Follow him! Catch up with him! Don’t leave him alone for a minute!” she said in a hurried whisper. “He’s mad! Don’t you know he’s mad? He’s in a fever, a nervous fever. The doctor told me so. Go, run after him....”
Alyosha jumped up and ran after Ivan, who was not yet fifty paces ahead of him.
“What do you want?” Ivan turned on him sharply, seeing that he was running after him. “She told you to catch up with me because I’m mad. I know it all by heart,” he added irritably.
“She’s mistaken, of course. But she’s right that you’re ill,” said Alyosha. “I was looking at your face just now. You look very ill, Ivan.”
Ivan walked on without stopping. Alyosha followed him.
“And do you know, Alexey Fyodorovitch, how people go out of their minds?” Ivan asked, in a voice that had suddenly become quiet, without a trace of irritation, with a note of the simplest curiosity.
“No, I don’t. I suppose there are all kinds of madness.”
“And can a man see for himself that he’s going mad?”
“I imagine a man can’t see himself clearly in such circumstances,” Alyosha answered in surprise.
Ivan was silent for half a minute.
“If you want to talk to me, please change the subject,” he said suddenly.

“Oh, while I think of it, I have a letter for you,” said Alyosha timidly. He took Lise’s note from his pocket and held it out to Ivan. They were just under a lamp-post. Ivan recognized the handwriting at once.
“Ah, from that little demon!” he laughed spitefully. Without opening the envelope, he tore it into bits and threw them in the air. The wind scattered the pieces.
“She isn’t even sixteen yet, I believe, and already she’s offering herself,” he said contemptuously, striding on down the street again.
“What do you mean, offering herself?” exclaimed Alyosha.
“The way loose women offer themselves, of course.”

“How can you, Ivan, how can you?” Alyosha cried warmly, in a grieved voice. “She’s a child! You’re insulting a child! She’s ill. She’s very ill, too. She may be on the verge of madness herself.... I had hoped to hear something from you ... that would save her.”
“You’ll hear nothing from me. If she’s a child, I’m not her nurse. Be quiet, Alexey. Don’t go on about her. I’m not even thinking about it.”
They were silent again for a moment.
“She’ll be praying all night now to the Mother of God to show her how to act tomorrow at the trial,” he said sharply and angrily again.
“You ... you mean Katerina Ivanovna?”

“Yes. Whether she’s to save Mitya or ruin him. She’ll pray for light from above. She can’t make up her own mind, you see. She hasn’t had time to decide yet. She takes me for her nurse, too. She wants me to sing her lullabies.”
“Katerina Ivanovna loves you, brother,” said Alyosha sadly.
“Maybe. But I’m not very keen on her.”

“She’s suffering. Why do you ... sometimes say things to her that give her hope?” Alyosha went on, with timid reproach. “I know you’ve given her hope. Forgive me for speaking to you like this,” he added.

“I can’t behave toward her as I ought to—break it off completely and tell her so straight out,” said Ivan irritably. “I have to wait until sentence is passed on the murderer. If I break with her now, she’ll take revenge on me by ruining that scoundrel tomorrow at the trial, because she hates him and knows she hates him. It’s all a lie—lie upon lie! As long as I don’t break with her, she goes on hoping, and she won’t ruin that monster, since she knows how much I want to get him out of trouble. If only that damned verdict would come!”
The words “murderer” and “monster” echoed painfully in Alyosha’s heart.
“But how can she ruin Mitya?” he asked, thinking over Ivan’s words. “What evidence can she give that would ruin Mitya?”
“You don’t know that yet. She has a document in her hands, in Mitya’s own handwriting, that proves conclusively that he did murder Fyodor Pavlovitch.”
“That’s impossible!” cried Alyosha.
“Why is it impossible? I’ve read it myself.”
“There can’t be such a document!” Alyosha repeated warmly. “There can’t be, because he’s not the murderer. It wasn’t he who murdered father, not he!”
Ivan suddenly stopped.
“Who is the murderer, then, in your opinion?” he asked, with apparent coldness. There was even a haughty note in his voice.
“You know who,” Alyosha said in a low, penetrating voice.
“Who? You mean that myth about the crazy idiot, the epileptic, Smerdyakov?”
Alyosha suddenly felt himself trembling all over.
“You know who,” broke helplessly from him. He could scarcely breathe.
“Who? Who?” Ivan cried, almost fiercely. All his restraint suddenly vanished.
“I only know one thing,” Alyosha went on, still almost in a whisper, “_it wasn’t you_ who killed father.”
“‘Not you’! What do you mean, ‘not you’?” Ivan was thunderstruck.
“It was not you who killed father, not you!” Alyosha repeated firmly.
The silence lasted half a minute.
“I know I didn’t. Are you raving?” said Ivan, with a pale, twisted smile. His eyes were riveted on Alyosha. They were standing under a lamp-post again.
“No, Ivan. You’ve told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”
“When did I say so? I was in Moscow.... When have I said so?” Ivan stammered helplessly.

“You’ve said so to yourself many times, when you’ve been alone during these two dreadful months,” Alyosha went on, as softly and distinctly as before. Yet he was speaking now, as it were, not of himself, not by his own will, but obeying some irresistible command. “You have accused yourself, and you have confessed to yourself that you are the murderer and no one else. But you didn’t do it. You’re mistaken. You are not the murderer. Do you hear? It was not you! God has sent me to tell you so.”

They were both silent. The silence lasted a whole long minute. They stood still, gazing into each other’s eyes. They were both pale. Suddenly Ivan began trembling all over and clutched Alyosha’s shoulder.
“You’ve been in my room!” he whispered hoarsely. “You were there at night, when he came.... Confess ... have you seen him, have you seen him?”
“Who do you mean—Mitya?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.
“Not him, damn the monster!” Ivan shouted in a frenzy. “Do you know that he visits me? How did you find out? Speak!”
“Who is _he_? I don’t know who you’re talking about,” Alyosha faltered, beginning to be alarmed.
“Yes, you do know ... or how could you—? It’s impossible that you don’t know.”
Suddenly he seemed to check himself. He stood still and seemed to think. A strange grin twisted his lips.

“Brother,” Alyosha began again, in a shaking voice, “I’ve said this to you because you’ll believe my word. I know that. I tell you once and for all, it’s not you. Do you hear, once and for all! God has put it into my heart to say this to you, even if it makes you hate me from this hour.”
But by now Ivan had apparently regained his self-control.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” he said, with a cold smile, “I can’t endure prophets and epileptics—messengers from God especially—and you know that only too well. I break off all relations with you from this moment, and probably for good. Please leave me at this turning. It’s the way to your lodgings, too. And you’d better be particularly careful not to come to me today! Do you hear?”
He turned and walked on with a firm step, not looking back.
“Brother,” Alyosha called after him, “if anything happens to you today, turn to me before anyone else!”

But Ivan made no reply. Alyosha stood under the lamp-post at the crossroads until Ivan had vanished into the darkness. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan were living in lodgings. Neither of them was willing to live in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s empty house. Alyosha had a furnished room in the house of some working people. Ivan lived some distance away. He had taken a roomy and fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house that belonged to a well-to-do lady, the widow of an official. But his only attendant was a deaf and rheumatic old crone who went to bed at six every evening and got up at six in the morning. Ivan had become remarkably indifferent to his comforts lately, and very fond of being alone. He did everything for himself in the one room he lived in, and rarely entered any of the other rooms of the lodge.

He reached the gate of the house and had his hand on the bell when he suddenly stopped. He felt that he was trembling all over with anger. All at once he let go of the bell, turned back with a curse, and walked off rapidly in the opposite direction. He walked a mile and a half to a tiny, slanting wooden house, almost a hut, where Marya Kondratyevna was now lodging. She was the neighbor who used to come to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s kitchen for soup, and Smerdyakov had once sung her his songs and played the guitar for her. She had sold their little house and was living here with her mother. Smerdyakov, who was ill—almost dying—had been with them ever since Fyodor Pavlovitch’s death. It was to him that Ivan was going now, drawn by a sudden and irresistible prompting.
